name: WEEE Directive
evidence_rating: moderate: the Commission evaluation and a European Court of Auditors review measure collection and recycling; an EU-wide study of e-waste flows; panel studies of collection schemes; no causal estimate of the Directive itself
summary: The Commission's 2025 evaluation found that collection of waste electronics rose by about 65% between 2012 and 2021, but that nearly half of all e-waste generated in the EU is still not collected and only three Member States met the 65% collection target in 2022. The European Court of Auditors (2021) found that collected e-waste is mostly recycled but that collection lags, and an EU-funded study estimated that only 35% of Europe's e-waste went through official channels in 2012, with 1.3 million tonnes leaving the EU undocumented.

indicators.objective: No monitoring indicators set in the proposal; assessed through the Commission's reports listed below

indicators.target_or_baseline: 65% of EEE placed on the market (or 85% of WEEE generated) from 2019
indicators.evidence: Collection up about 65% (2012-2021); nearly half of WEEE generated not collected; three Member States met the target in 2022.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Evaluation of Directive 2012/19/EU on waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE), Commission staff working document (July 2025)
literature.title: Evaluation of Directive 2012/19/EU on waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE)
literature.method: ex-post evaluation (Member State data, supporting study by Ramboll, Umweltbundesamt and Oeko-Institut, consultation)
literature.headline: Collection up about 65% between 2012 and 2021, but nearly half of WEEE not collected; only three Member States met the 65% target in 2022; recycling targets do not drive recovery of critical raw materials
literature.summary_plain: The Commission found more e-waste is collected than before, but most countries miss the target and valuable materials are still lost.

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2021), Review 04/2021: EU actions and existing challenges on electronic waste, European Court of Auditors
literature.title: Review 04/2021: EU actions and existing challenges on electronic waste
literature.method: review of Eurostat data, studies and legislation
literature.outcomes: collection rates vs targets; recovery/recycling; illegal shipments
literature.headline: Over 2012-2018 more than 87% of collected WEEE was recovered and over 80% recycled, but Member States collect less than half the weight of EEE placed on the market. Few reached the 65% target in 2017-2018, and only Bulgaria and Croatia were estimated to reach it in 2019.
literature.summary_plain: The EU's auditors found that e-waste which is collected is mostly recycled, but most countries miss the collection target and illegal shipments remain a problem.
literature.quality: descriptive; official audit body; not causal

literature.citation: Huisman, J.; Botezatu, I.; Herreras, L.; et al. (CWIT consortium: UNU, INTERPOL, UNICRI, WEEE Forum, et al.) (2015), Countering WEEE Illegal Trade (CWIT) Summary Report: Market Assessment, Legal Analysis, Crime Analysis and Recommendations Roadmap, CWIT project report (EU FP7), Lyon
literature.authors: Huisman, J.; Botezatu, I.; Herreras, L.; et al. (CWIT consortium: UNU, INTERPOL, UNICRI, WEEE Forum, et al.)
literature.title: Countering WEEE Illegal Trade (CWIT) Summary Report: Market Assessment, Legal Analysis, Crime Analysis and Recommendations Roadmap
literature.method: mass-balance market assessment of e-waste flows, legal and crime analysis
literature.outcomes: share of e-waste officially collected; exports; non-compliant recycling
literature.headline: Only 35% (3.3 million tonnes) of e-waste discarded in Europe in 2012 ended up in official collection and recycling. The other 65% (6.15 Mt) was exported (1.5 Mt), recycled under non-compliant conditions in Europe (3.15 Mt), scavenged (0.75 Mt) or binned (0.75 Mt), and 1.3 Mt left the EU as undocumented exports.
literature.summary_plain: Ten years into the WEEE regime, roughly two thirds of Europe's e-waste was escaping the official system, mostly through poor-quality recycling inside Europe rather than export.
literature.interested_party: consortium includes WEEE Forum (producer compliance schemes)

literature.citation: Favot, M.; Grassetti, L.; Massarutto, A.; Veit, R. (2022), Regulation and competition in the extended producer responsibility models: Results in the WEEE sector in Europe, Waste Management 145:60-71
literature.authors: Favot, M.; Grassetti, L.; Massarutto, A.; Veit, R.
literature.title: Regulation and competition in the extended producer responsibility models: Results in the WEEE sector in Europe
literature.method: panel econometrics on an original database of European compliance schemes
literature.outcomes: cost of WEEE management for given collection outcomes
literature.headline: Finds 'significant evidence that a more competitive market structure allows achieving the same collection outcomes at a lower cost' across European WEEE EPR systems.
literature.summary_plain: Within the WEEE Directive's framework, countries with competing producer compliance schemes collect e-waste more cheaply.
literature.quality: econometric (panel associations) on national implementation choices; not a causal estimate of the Directive itself

literature.citation: Corsini, F.; Rizzi, F.; Frey, M. (2017), Extended producer responsibility: The impact of organizational dimensions on WEEE collection from households, Waste Management 59:23-29
literature.authors: Corsini, F.; Rizzi, F.; Frey, M.
literature.title: Extended producer responsibility: The impact of organizational dimensions on WEEE collection from households
literature.method: latent class analysis of Member States' transposition and EPR organisational settings vs household collection
literature.headline: Finds 'a strong connection between allocation of responsibility and organizational model adopted in Member States' and collection performance for small household equipment. It highlights the role of clearing houses in moderating 'short-sighted competition' between collective schemes.
literature.summary_plain: How countries organise producer responsibility under the Directive strongly affects how much household e-waste they collect.

literature.citation: Favot, M.; Grassetti, L. (2017), E-waste collection in Italy: Results from an exploratory analysis, Waste Management 67:222-231
literature.title: E-waste collection in Italy: Results from an exploratory analysis
literature.method: stochastic frontier panel model, 20 Italian regions, 2008-2015
literature.outcomes: kg of household WEEE collected per inhabitant
literature.headline: A 1% increase in collection points corresponds to a 0.25% increase in collection, and Southern regions collect 0.66 times as much as Central ones. Performance improved steadily after a very low 2008, mainly due to more collection points.
literature.summary_plain: In Italy, e-waste collection under the WEEE system rose over time, driven mainly by more drop-off points.
